title: When Should a Commercial HVAC System Be Replaced?
h1: When Should You Replace Your Commercial HVAC System?
description: Replace commercial HVAC when repairs pile up, energy costs climb, comfort complaints grow or units near the end of their life. Here's how to plan for it.
quick_answer: Plan to replace a commercial HVAC system when units approach the end of their expected life, repairs become frequent or expensive, energy costs keep rising, comfort complaints increase or the equipment uses phased-out refrigerant like R-22. Most rooftop units last roughly 15 to 20 years with good maintenance. Planned replacement avoids costly downtime.
body:
For a business, HVAC failure isn't just uncomfortable. It can close a dining room, spoil inventory, shut down a server closet or send employees home. That's why replacing commercial equipment on your own schedule is almost always better than waiting for it to fail in the middle of a heat wave.

How long do commercial HVAC systems last?

Lifespan depends on the type of equipment, how hard it works and how well it's maintained. As a rough guide:

  • Packaged rooftop units: roughly 15 to 20 years
  • Split systems: roughly 15 to 20 years
  • Ductless and VRF systems: similar, with good maintenance
  • Chillers and boilers: often longer, and more common in larger buildings

In coastal areas, salt air shortens the life of rooftop units by corroding coils, cabinets and electrical connections. Units on hot inland roofs run long hours in summer, which adds wear to compressors and fans.

What are the signs it's time to replace?

  • Frequent breakdowns. Several repair calls a year, or the same problem coming back.
  • Major component failure. A failed compressor, cracked heat exchanger or badly corroded coil on an older unit.
  • Rising energy costs. Utility bills climbing without a change in use or hours.
  • Comfort complaints. Hot and cold spots, poor humidity control or zones that never reach setpoint.
  • Old refrigerant. Units using R-22, which is no longer produced, are costly to recharge.
  • Air quality issues. Persistent odors, dust or poor ventilation that maintenance doesn't solve.
  • Changes in how you use the space. A new tenant, more equipment or more people may need more capacity.

Should you repair or replace?

A common approach is to compare the repair cost to the value left in the unit. If a unit is near the end of its expected life and needs a major repair, replacement usually makes more sense. If it's younger and the repair is moderate, repairing is often the right move.

It also helps to look at your whole building, not just one unit. If you have several rooftop units of the same age, planning to replace them in phases over a couple of years can spread out the cost and avoid a string of emergency failures.

What should you consider when choosing new equipment?

  1. Proper sizing. A load calculation based on current use, occupancy and equipment, not just the old unit's tonnage.
  2. Efficiency. Higher-efficiency units and economizers can lower operating costs, especially for buildings that run long hours.
  3. Refrigerant. New equipment uses newer refrigerants as older ones are phased down. Ask about service and parts for whatever you choose.
  4. Controls. Programmable or networked thermostats help avoid conditioning an empty building.
  5. Coastal protection. Corrosion-resistant coil coatings for buildings near the ocean.
  6. Ventilation and filtration. Make sure the system meets ventilation needs and can handle better filters during wildfire smoke events.
  7. Roof and structural work. New units may need curb adapters, a crane lift or electrical changes.

How do you plan a replacement with minimal disruption?

Good planning keeps your business running:

  • Schedule work in spring or fall, when you can go a day without cooling or heat
  • Coordinate with the building owner or property manager early
  • Plan crane lifts and roof work for early mornings or weekends when needed
  • Replace units one at a time in multi-unit buildings so some spaces stay conditioned
  • Include ductwork inspection and cleaning so new equipment isn't pushing old dust

How does maintenance affect replacement timing?

Many businesses only think about HVAC when something breaks. But equipment that's checked on a schedule rarely surprises you. A technician who sees your units every season can tell you which ones are healthy, which are slipping and which should go into next year's budget.

A maintenance plan with regular filter changes, coil cleaning, belt checks and refrigerant checks extends equipment life and gives you an early warning when a unit is near the end. Service records also help you make replacement decisions based on facts, not guesswork.

faqs: How long does a commercial rooftop unit last?

Most packaged rooftop units last roughly 15 to 20 years with regular maintenance. Units near the coast may wear out sooner because of salt air corrosion, and units that run long hours in hot inland areas may need replacement earlier.
Can commercial HVAC be replaced without shutting down my business?

Usually, with planning. Work can be scheduled for off-hours, and in buildings with multiple units, replacing one at a time keeps most of the space conditioned. Your contractor should give you a clear schedule in advance.
Is it worth replacing all rooftop units at once?
Sometimes. Replacing them together can simplify the project and crane work. If budget is a concern, a phased plan that replaces the oldest or least reliable units first is a practical alternative.
